value.title: Aspect is not a fixed property of linguistic expressions

titleRich.content: Aspect is not a fixed property of linguistic expressions

abstract.content: Telicity and durativity are commonly taken to be fixed properties of sense- and structurally disambiguated expressions—generally, of verb phrases or clauses. We show that this assumption requires revision. Using data from two experiments aimed at measuring telicity and durativity by operationalizing standard diagnostics, we derive measures of telicity and durativity for expressions headed by 40 verb forms spanning seven semantic classes. We construct these expressions to instantiate particular verb senses and find substantial within-sense variability in both telicity and durativity, even for verb classes prior work treats as aspectually stable. In a similarity judgment task on the same materials, we find that this within-sense variability registers in how speakers judge the similarity of two event descriptions: the more two descriptions match aspectually on our measures, the more similar they are rated, with this effect being stronger within sense than across sense. These results suggest that lexical aspect is not a fixed property of expressions but that comprehenders have fine-grained knowledge of the distribution of possible aspectual construals for an expression.
